title: Colombian water safety
text:
What the colour means
    IRCA (Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano) is a 0–100 risk score built from
      the year's surveillance samples. 0 is no risk; 100 is unfit for consumption. Resolución 2115 de 2007
      sorts it into five bands. The numbers on this page are IRCA (utility-supplied, INS open data):
      they come from the water providers' (prestadores) reports, not from INS's own national total.
    

    Tunja: one city, two kinds of tap
    
    
      Tunja, IRCA (utility-supplied, INS open data), urban and rural zones, 2010–2023. Shaded bands are the Resolución 2115 risk bands.
    

    Is Tunja typical for Boyacá?
    
    
      UrbanRural
    
    
      Share of Boyacá's 123 municipalities in each IRCA (utility-supplied, INS open data) band, by year. Grey is no reported IRCA, not "safe".

    Piped water is not the same as safe water
    Coverage counts connections to an aqueduct. IRCA scores what comes out of it. The two answer different questions,
      and Tunja shows why they must be read side by side.
    
      Tunja, aqueduct and sewerage coverage for the whole municipality (REC, Superservicios via DNP TerriData). Department capitals have no urban/rural split. Nothing here is filled.
    

    How to read this without fooling yourself
    
      Descriptive, not causal. Nothing here shows that water quality changes any outcome. Altitude, poverty (IPM, census 2018), rurality, municipal finances and which systems get sampled all move together with IRCA and could explain patterns on their own.
      Rural IRCA is missing far more often than urban IRCA, and the sampled systems can change from year to year. A rural drop or rise may reflect which systems were sampled, not the water itself.
      Utility-supplied. This IRCA comes from prestadores reports in the INS open table (nxt2-39c3).
      Relief is stylised. Block height is SRTM elevation at the head-town coordinates (derived, not an official DANE altitude), applied to the whole municipality.
      Rainfall is CHIRPS v3.0 annual precipitation averaged over each municipal polygon. Drop counts are a visual proxy for rainfall × area, not a measure of water supply.
      Infant mortality (shown in the side panel only) changes method in 2017 and is volatile for small municipalities.
    
    Sources: INS IRCA (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3); DNP TerriData; DANE DIVIPOLA, projections and MGN 2023 boundaries; CHIRPS v3.0; SRTM via OpenTopoData. Derived table: visuals/boyaca.json, built by scripts/visuals_data.py from data/. 3D with three.js.

title: Water safety and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities, 2016-2023
text:
Summary
Using 11,235 municipality-zone-year rows (1,090 municipalities, 2016-2023), k-means finds 4 groups of municipal water profiles. The one with the highest utility-supplied IRCA (median np.float64(35.2)) is “Rural, low-coverage, high-risk water”. Infant mortality, Saber 11 scores and dropout differ across clusters, but these are descriptive associations, not causal effects of water quality.


Question
How do Colombian municipalities group by the safety of their drinking water and the context around it, and how do infant mortality, school results and dropout look in each group?


Data
One row is a municipality x zone (urban/rural) x year, from the public dataset in data/ (INS, DNP TerriData, DANE, CHIRPS, ICFES, MEN; see Sources). IRCA is the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA from INS open data, not INS’s national total; it runs from 0 (no risk) to 100 (unfit) and is much more often missing for rural zones. Only rows of municipalities with an IRCA value in 2016-2023 are used. Department capitals have no urban/rural coverage split, so their urban coverage is filled from the municipal total (214 rows, flagged in the data).


Method
Nine profile features (IRCA, water and sewer coverage, multidimensional poverty, rural share, altitude, rainfall, municipal performance, log water transfers per person) were standardised within each year and clustered with k-means (random_state = 42, 20 starts). k = 4 was chosen from the elbow, with silhouette 0.19 and stability across five seeds (ARI >= 0.999). Outcomes (infant mortality, Saber 11, dropout) were not used to cluster; they only describe the clusters.


What sets the clusters apart








Figure 1: Cluster mean z-scores (within year) of the nine profile features; blue is below the yearly average and red above.







Outcomes by cluster








Figure 2: Median infant mortality (per 1,000 live births), Saber 11 mean score and school dropout (%) by cluster and year. Lines break where a source has no data.





Infant mortality changes method in 2017 and Saber 11 has no data for 2018 and 2021, so year-to-year changes should not be read as real trends.


Correlation is not causation








Figure 3: Median infant mortality (per 1,000 live births) by IRCA band (utility-supplied) within each cluster. Bars are medians; the Spearman rho between IRCA and infant mortality is in the legend.





Within each cluster the association between IRCA and infant mortality is weak (rho from -0.04 to 0.10). This is descriptive and does not establish a causal effect of water safety. Poverty, health services, altitude and rurality may confound it.


Limits

Utility-supplied IRCA only; rural zones are often unsampled.
Infant mortality changes method in 2017 and is volatile in small municipalities.
Saber 11 covers 2014-2017, 2019, 2020 and 2022; school location is not residence.
Missing coverage was imputed (year x zone median) in 653 rows.
Clusters are descriptive groupings, not causal categories.



Sources

INS, “Calidad del Agua para Consumo Humano en Colombia” (IRCA), datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3.
DNP, TerriData (coverage, rurality, IPM, MDM, IDF, SGP, infant mortality), https://terridata.dnp.gov.co.
DANE, DIVIPOLA gdxc-w37w and population projections, https://www.dane.gov.co.
CHIRPS v3.0 rainfall, https://doi.org/10.15780/G2JQ0P.
NASA SRTM via OpenTopoData, https://doi.org/10.5067/MEaSUREs/SRTM/SRTMGL3.003.
ICFES Saber 11, datos.gov.co kgxf-xxbe, rnvb-vnyh; MEN dropout, nudc-7mev.
Details: data/README.md. Resolución 2115 de 2007, art. 15 (IRCA bands).

title: Four kinds of municipal zone
text:
K-means on nine profile features (utility-supplied IRCA, coverage, poverty, rurality, altitude, rainfall, performance, water transfers) finds 4 kinds of municipal zone among 11,235 municipality-zone-year rows, 2016-2023:



Cities and large towns, no-risk water (median IRCA 1.6, 284 municipalities)
Highland towns, no-risk water (median IRCA 4.0, 558 municipalities)
Lowland towns, low-risk water (median IRCA 9.2, 479 municipalities)
Rural, low-coverage, high-risk water (median IRCA 35.2, 729 municipalities)



Outcomes (infant mortality, Saber 11, dropout) did not enter the clustering. They differ across clusters, but this is descriptive and does not establish a causal effect of water quality. Details: clusters and the report.

title: Clusters of municipal water profiles
text:
Clusters group municipality x zone x year rows (2016-2023) by profile features only (IRCA, coverage, rurality, altitude, rainfall, poverty, fiscal and performance indices). IRCA is utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA from INS open data. Outcomes were not used.
Figure 1: Elbow plot: k-means inertia for k = 2 to 8. The curve flattens after k = 4.
Figure 2: Mean silhouette score by k. Higher means better-separated clusters; all values are modest (below 0.25).
Figure 3: First two principal components of the standardised profile features, coloured by cluster. Descriptive grouping only.

section: What this does and does not show
text:
What this does and does not show

Shows: municipalities fall into four water-and-context profiles; outcomes differ by profile
Does not show: that water quality causes any outcome
Confounders: poverty, health services, altitude, rurality
Gaps: infant mortality method changes in 2017; Saber 11 has no 2018 or 2021
